newsitem.title: USA: U.S. admiral says strike is warning to Iraq.
newsitem.headline: U.S. admiral says strike is warning to Iraq.

text.p: U.S. forces fired 27 sea- and air-launched cruise missiles at military targets in southern Iraq on Tuesday as a warning to Baghdad to comply with Gulf War ceasefire resolutions, an American admiral said.

"The strikes were ordered as a warning to Iraq to adhere to requirements outlined in United Nations resolutions," Rear Admiral Edward Moore, commander of U.S. naval forces in the Gulf, told reporters aboard the aircraft carrier Carl Vinson.

Giving details of what he called operation "Desert Strike", Moore said 13 missiles were fired from two B-52 bombers flying from Guam in the Pacific and 14 were fired from the USS Laboon guided missile destroyer and the USS Shilo cruiser in the Gulf.
"At 7.15 this morning (04.15 GMT) U.S. naval and air forces executed air strikes against Iraqi military sites," he said.

"The strikes were conducted with both shipboard-launched Tomahawk cruise missiles and conventional air launched cruise missiles and were directed against Iraqi air defence sites and command and control facilities," Moore said.
In Washington, defence officials said the U.S. raids were launched on orders from President Bill Clinton in retaliation for Iraqi military attacks against Kurds.

"Yes, it is in response to those events," Moore replied when asked if the strike was connected to Iraqi attacks on Kurds. Iraqi troops at the weekend intervened in Kurdish factional fighting in the country's north to support one group against the other.
Asked if he knew of any retaliation by Iraq, Moore replied: "I dont know of any firing or any response by Iraq."

The two B-52s were escorted by a total complement of 12 F-14 and F-14D warplanes from the Carl Vinson, which exercised command and control of the strike, with four warplanes flying with the bombers at any one time, Moore said.

"We are always in a state of readiness to respond to any contingencies that might come up," Moore said. "I don't want to go beyond what kind of state of readiness it is but we are always prepared to respond to any contingency."

Officers said the Carl Vinson battlegroup in the Gulf comprised the carrier itself, one supply ship, three cruisers, one frigate and one submarine. But they declined to say how many other U.S. warships were in the waterway.

Moore, in response to questions, added he felt U.S. forces in the Gulf were not in particular danger. "I dont feel that any U.S. forces in the Gulf are in any particular danger. The strike for this morning has been completed," he said.
